segments.text: Imagine you are a scribe in the 1450s.
All day, you hand-copy the king's proclamations
and send them out across the kingdom.
It is a reliable, steady job.
Then one morning, you hear that a guy in minds
built a new machine.
It prints pages a thousand times faster
than you can write them by hand.
You have two choices.
You can pretend the new technology isn't happening,
or you can learn the machine well enough to operate it.
This board illustrates our modern version of that story.
AI is the press in this comparison,
and learning to use it is today's version
of learning to run that new machine.
Run it, or someone else will.
AI left the realm of science fiction years ago
to become part of your daily routine.
It operates the apps on your phone
and powers the tools your first job will hand you on day one.
Most of what it does today, it will do better tomorrow.
This graphic shows a breakdown of exactly where AI
already lives in your daily routine.
First, it recommends media by predicting
what you might like next.
You interact with this on Spotify, Netflix, and TikTok.
Second, navigation tools predict traffic
and your arrival time on apps like Google Maps and Waze.
Third, face recognition validates your identity,
checking whether a face matches you
for phone unlocks and photo tagging.
Fourth, voice assistants turn your speech
into words when you talk to Siri, Alexa, or Hey Google.
Finally, chatbots carry on direct conversations with you
through programs like Chat GPT, Claude, and Gemini.
Looking at this complete picture shows us something clear.
AI was already part of your day before chatbots arrived.
Because you already interact with these systems,
you can easily shift from being a passive consumer
to an active user.
You can start now.
Learn what AI does well, notice where it struggles,
and practice using it for something you care about.
Every project gives you experience
you can bring to the next one.
We have seen tools close the gap between ideas
and creation before.
Before personal computers, becoming a designer
meant spending years at a drafting table,
learning to draw every line by hand.
Then, desktop publishing arrived.
Suddenly, a teenager with a personal computer
could design posters, magazines, and brochures
from their bedroom.
The tool didn't replace skill.
Instead, it shortened the distance
between wanting to do the work and actually doing it.
AI gives you a similar chance to start making things
while you build your skills.
This infographic maps out three specific reasons
why you'll thrive in the AI future
if you begin learning now.
First, this is your time.
Building skills while you are in school
provides a safe environment to try new things,
ask questions, and learn from the results.
Second, you'll move faster.
AI helps you try out ideas, get immediate feedback,
and tackle projects you otherwise wouldn't know how to start.
Third, you build good habits early.
Starting now means you practice asking good questions,
checking answers, and making your own independent decisions.
Start now.
Build skills you'll carry into whatever comes next.
New tools consistently change how people work.
The steam engine proved this by replacing human
and animal physical labor.
Electricity followed, accelerating factory production
and increasing output.
The internet then shifted how we process
and distribute information across a global network.
AI could do it across almost everything.
This scale is recognized at the highest levels.
In July 2025, the White House released
an official national strategy document
titled Winning the Race, America's AI Action Plan.
The document outlines the scope of this technology clearly.
An industrial revolution, an information revolution,
and a renaissance, all at once.
This is the potential that AI presents.
AI is today's printing press.
Learn to run it.
